Concealment and reliability
Don’t put the relay next to the alarm unit or in plain sight: that’s where it will be looked for first.
Run the wires along the factory harness and wrap them the same way as the factory harness so the new connection doesn’t stand out.

The spot must be dry and protected from dust, where the relay won’t get kicked or snagged during cleaning: a contact corroded by cold and dust is a common cause of a no-start a year after installation.
The relay must not dangle: secure it to the harness with a zip tie. All connections — soldered and insulated, no twisted splices.
Record the relay location and the circuit in your own archive along with photos of the installation: a year later it will save hours of searching.

An NC relay (30–87a) opens the circuit on the alarm’s command; an NO relay (30–87) keeps the circuit closed while the alarm allows it.
Interrupt the fuel pump circuit or the starter control circuit; leave safety circuits and the factory immobilizer alone.
The kill must never trigger while driving; the relay contact must be reliable, the joints soldered.
The relay — rated with margin, hidden, in a dry place, secured; circuit current flows only through the relay contacts.

Pump current flows through the normally closed contact the whole drive. A bad contact weakens or stops the pump, and the engine dies. That’s why the relay must be good quality and the joints soldered.

Normally closed — NC, contacts 30 and 87a. At rest the circuit is closed and the car works as if there were no alarm. To kill, the alarm energizes the coil and the contact opens. A regular relay coil draws about 0.1–0.15 A, so it is not kept energized for the whole time the car is parked: the kill output is set to switch on only when someone tries to start the car while it is armed — the system's manual says how.

Pin switches only notice that a door, the hood or the trunk was opened — that’s covered in the lesson on pin switches. Sensors guard the car when everything is closed. The shock sensor hears a hit to the body or glass, the tilt sensor — jacking or loading onto a tow truck, the interior motion sensor — movement in the cabin. Where the sensors go and how they are set decides whether the alarm protects the car or wakes up the neighborhood at night.
Shock sensor: two zones

Inside the sensor is a sensing element: a piezo element, a magnet over a coil or, in newer systems, an accelerometer chip. A hit becomes an electrical signal, and the sensor compares it with two thresholds. A light hit crosses only the warning-zone threshold: the siren gives a short chirp and the turn signals flash. A hard hit crosses the alarm-zone threshold too: a full alarm, and on systems with GSM a message to the phone as well. A separate sensor has its own output for each zone, usually a negative one: at rest the zone wire carries a voltage held by the control unit, and when the sensor trips it briefly pulls the wire to ground, so the unit sees a pulse.
A light hit crosses only the warning threshold; a hard hit crosses the alarm threshold too.

Where to mount the sensor
On a rigid part of the body or a sturdy factory bracket under the dash, close to the middle of the car: that way the sensor hears hits from both sides equally.
Screw the housing down or strap it tight to the bracket. A sensor hanging on its wires sometimes misses a hit and sometimes trips by itself when it swings.
Not on thin plastic and not next to anything that shakes — small motors, the heater blower: the sensor will take their vibration for a hit.
The sensitivity knob should stay reachable for adjustment, but out of sight.
If the shock and tilt sensor is built into the control unit, as in many modern systems, all of these rules apply to where the unit itself goes.

Airbag harnesses run under the dash — they have yellow connectors and often a yellow sleeve. Don’t fasten sensors or their wires to them, don’t splice anything into them, and don’t put sensors where an airbag deploys.
Setting the sensitivity
Start with low sensitivity. The knob is on the sensor housing; built-in sensors are set from the fob, in the app or with software — per your system’s manual.
Arm the car and wait for the sensors to come on: many systems have a delay after arming.
Test it: a light slap with your palm on a body pillar or a tire should give a warning, a harder one an alarm. Don’t hit the glass, and don’t kick the car.
Raise the sensitivity a little at a time and test after every step — on both sides of the car, front and rear.
If the sensor has a separate knob for each zone, the alarm zone must stay noticeably less sensitive than the warning zone.
A good setting: a truck driving past doesn’t trigger an alarm, but the sensor hears a light palm slap.
Tilt and interior motion sensors

The tilt sensor remembers the car’s position when it’s armed and raises the alarm if the position changes: the car is jacked up or loaded onto a tow truck. It ignores slow changes — snow on the roof, tires that have cooled down. It’s mounted rigidly to the body, in the orientation the manual requires.

A microwave interior motion sensor “sees” movement in the cabin and a little around the car — through the glass. It has two zones too: the outer one — someone walked right up — gives a warning, the inner one — a hand inside the cabin — an alarm. It goes near the center of the cabin, for example in the tunnel between the seats, away from metal.

An ultrasonic interior sensor — a transmitter and receiver pair up by the headliner, usually near the dome light — watches the air in the closed cabin. It only works with the windows and sunroof closed.
The motion sensor’s outer zone gives a warning, the inner zone an alarm.

False alarms
Wind and vibration: gusts rock the car, trucks or a streetcar go by, construction is going on nearby. A less sensitive setting helps, especially on tall vehicles and cars with a roof rack.
The sensor is loosely mounted or hangs on its wires — it swings.

A “floating” ground: the sensor or unit ground is on a painted or rusty bolt, or there’s a poor contact in a connector. The unit takes the noise on its input for a trigger. Clean the spot and tighten the ground, as in the lesson on unit power and ground.
A chafed zone wire touches the body — to the unit that’s the same “to ground” signal as the sensor tripping.

For the motion sensor — anything that moves in the closed cabin: a toy or air freshener on the mirror, sunshades, insects, airflow from the heater or a parking heater. For the ultrasonic one — also a window or sunroof left slightly open.
Sometimes false alarms show up only in freezing weather or only in the heat: then recheck the setting in that season.
When to bypass the sensors

Sometimes the car needs to be locked with the sensors bypassed for a while: a dog or cat stays in the cabin, a parking heater or the heater blower is running, the sunroof is open, the car is carried on a tow truck or a ferry. For this, systems let you bypass the sensors or individual zones from the fob or the app — exactly how is in your system’s manual. The pin switches and the engine kill keep working. If the system has remote start, many systems bypass the shock sensor on their own while the engine is running. Explain all this to the customer when you hand the car over.
If the alarm suddenly stops hearing hits or goes completely silent, I check the fuses first — both in the alarm wiring and the factory ones — and only then take panels off and turn knobs.

The siren, antenna and GSM module are how the alarm talks to the world: the siren to the street, the antenna to the fob, GSM to the owner’s phone. Where they go decides whether the siren is still heard after a few winters, whether the fob reaches the car from the parking lot, and whether alarm messages arrive on time.

Under the hood, in a protected spot — for example behind the headlight or by the fender, on a sturdy bracket: so the siren is hard to reach from above or below.
Horn facing down: water and dirt drain out instead of collecting inside. A siren with the horn up fills with water, and in winter with ice, and goes quiet.
Away from hot parts — the exhaust manifold, the turbo — and from anything that spins: the radiator fan, belts.

The wire runs in split loom along the factory harnesses and into the cabin through the factory firewall grommet. If you had to drill, fit a rubber grommet and sealant, as in the lesson on routing wires.
The siren ground goes to the body, on a cleaned spot, like the unit ground.

Fob antenna
The antenna module — the transceiver — is usually stuck to the inside of the windshield, near the top: from there it “sees” the farthest.
Away from metal — the body frame, metal parts and wiring — at the distance given in the manual. Metal nearby “eats” the range.

Not on metallized tint film and not on an athermal windshield with a coating: the radio signal gets through them poorly. Coated windshields often have an uncoated area, usually by the mirror — check where it is on the actual car.
Not right next to a dash cam or radar detector: their electronics cause interference.
Degrease the glass and stick it on in the warm: tape holds poorly on cold glass. In winter, warm up the cabin first.

The antenna wire runs under the pillar trim along the factory harness. Many cars have curtain airbags in the pillars and above the doors: don’t lay the wire over the curtain, fasten it so it can’t keep the curtain from deploying, and don’t touch its yellow connectors. Remove and refit the pillar trim as described in the car’s service manual.

Interference: lots of radio signals around — a big shopping-mall parking lot, power lines, industrial sites.

A pinched or cracked antenna wire — after careless reassembly of the trim.
With a two-way fob, the car’s reply comes through the same antenna: if it’s badly placed, the alarm notification won’t reach the owner.
Use a SIM card from a carrier with good coverage where the car is parked most: at home, at work. An underground garage may have no signal at all — check on site.
Credit and plan: no money or the data plan ran out — no calls, no messages and no data in the app. Suggest autopay to the customer.
The SIM PIN — per the system’s manual: many modules only work with a card that has no PIN.
A separate GSM antenna also goes away from metal. A GPS antenna needs to “see the sky”: put it under the plastic of the dash, not under metal.
Check the connection before reassembling the interior: a call or message to the module, the signal level in the app.

A GSM module draws noticeably more than a basic alarm, and over a long stand that tells on the battery. After installation, measure the parasitic draw as in the lesson on current leakage, and explain this to the customer at handover.
If the siren is silent or the alarm doesn’t respond to the fob, I check the fuses first — in the alarm wiring and the factory ones — and only then take off the trim and dig further.
Siren: under the hood in a protected spot, horn down, away from hot and spinning parts; wire in split loom, ground on cleaned body metal.
Antenna: high on the windshield, away from metal, metallized film and the dash cam; wire under the trim, clear of the curtain airbags.
Fob range is cut by metal, tint, interference, a low antenna and a weak battery; the box gives the range for ideal conditions.

It’s louder that way

A customer never notices good installation work. Bad work shows up months later: a twisted splice corrodes and the kill relay or central locking fails, a wire chafes through and blows a fuse, the unit knocks under the dash on every bump. The rules in this lesson save you from those comebacks.
Connections: solder, not twists

A twisted splice under tape corrodes over time: resistance grows, the joint heats up, voltage is lost — the lesson on wiring repair covers this in detail. An alarm install has a lot of connections, and each one is soldered or properly crimped. Use neutral flux, such as rosin: acid flux eats copper. Use a soldering iron powerful enough for the solder to flow, not sit in a blob.
Find the wire by measuring, as in the lessons on pin switches and central locking, and check it once more right before you splice in.
Strip a 1–1.5 cm window in the insulation without cutting the strands.
Spread the strands, push the stripped end of the new wire through the gap and wrap it around.
Solder it so the solder flows in between the strands, and let it cool without moving the wire.
Insulate: several layers of tape overlapping the insulation, cloth tape on top. Where heat shrink can be slipped on, use heat shrink.
Strap the tap wire to the factory wire with a zip tie so vibration doesn’t crack the solder joint.
Splicing in without a cut: window, strands, solder, insulation — and the tap wire on a zip tie.

Run the alarm wires along the factory harnesses and zip-tie them at short intervals — the harness must not sag.

Keep clear of everything that moves: pedals, the steering shaft and its U-joint under the dash, seat tracks and mechanisms, door, hood and trunk hinges. Wires go into a door only through the factory boot.
Under the hood keep clear of hot parts — the exhaust manifold and turbo — and don’t lay wires on the engine.
Don’t fasten wires to brake or fuel lines or to an adjustable steering column.

A wire rubbing on the steering shaft, a pedal or a metal edge will sooner or later wear through to the copper. A positive wire on the body is a short circuit: without a fuse it can catch fire, and with a fuse the car is left without the alarm, sometimes without starting. So not a single positive wire without a fuse at the source — as in the lesson on unit power and ground.
The unit: hidden and secure
Hide the control unit deep under the dash and not in the most obvious place: behind the glovebox and under the steering column are where people look first.
The spot must be dry: not on the floor, where meltwater from snowy boots gets in, and not under the windshield, where it may leak.
Zip-tie the unit to a sturdy harness or bracket, and wrap it in cloth tape where it could knock on metal. If the unit has a built-in shock sensor, mount it rigidly, as in the lesson on sensors.
Wrap the wires from the unit the same way as the factory harness next to them — cloth tape or split loom — so they blend in.
Mount the kill relay separately from the unit, somewhere else along the harness, as in the lesson on engine immobilization.
Reassembly order
Reconnect the battery terminal and test all functions while the panels are off: that way a mistake is easy to fix.
Clear the cabin of wire, insulation and zip-tie offcuts.
Plug back in every factory connector you unplugged: switches, lights, sensors.
Refit the panels in reverse order and make sure no wires get caught under clips or screws. Replace broken clips.
Check the factory functions: power windows, lights, the instrument cluster, locks, the horn.
Drive over a rough road and listen: nothing should knock or rattle.

If something rattles after reassembly, look among the things you touched: the unit or a relay touching metal, a loose harness, a panel not fully clipped in. Wrap the unit and relays in cloth tape, zip-tie the harness, replace the clips. In freezing weather plastic is brittle: remove and refit trim in a heated bay, or the clips break and the panels squeak later.

After reassembly I hook up a scan tool and check whether any new codes have appeared in the modules — especially if the alarm is connected over CAN. Go with a Launch scan tool: it’s proven equipment, while cheap ELM327 adapters sometimes “knock the car out”.

The installation is finished, but don’t put the panels back yet: first the system is programmed and every function is tested — while everything is open, a mistake is easy to fix, as in the lesson on wire routing. Programming means learning the fobs and the owner’s phone, choosing the car model for the CAN module and setting the functions for the car and the customer. Menu names and button sequences differ from system to system, so everything is done per your system’s manual; here is the general order and what gets forgotten most often.
Fobs and phone
Fob learning mode is usually entered with the Valet button with the ignition on, then a button on the fob is pressed. The system confirms with a siren chirp or LED flashes.
Learn all the customer’s fobs in one session. On many systems, entering learning mode erases the old fobs from memory: learn one new fob and the rest stop working.
After learning, test each fob separately: arming, disarming and, on a two-way fob, the reply on the screen or by signal.

The owner’s phone is paired in the app or by command — per the manufacturer’s instructions, usually with the code from the owner’s card. Check that commands work and that the alarm notification arrives.
Learn all the customer’s fobs at once: on many systems a new session erases the old ones.

Manufacturer software and CAN

Many systems are set up in the manufacturer’s software on a computer or in the app. For the CAN module you choose the car’s make, model and year there — that decides which commands and statuses it understands, as in the lesson on the CAN bus during installation.
Firmware is updated only with the manufacturer’s official software, and the connection must not be interrupted while writing: a failure halfway through can brick the unit.
When everything is set, save the settings file to the installation archive if the software can do it. If the unit is replaced or reprogrammed, it can be loaded back.
Setting the functions
Central locking pulses — to suit the lock type: positive or negative, duration, double pulse to unlock, as in the lesson on central locking.
Door monitoring delay. If the pin switch wire is taken from the dome light circuit and the light fades out slowly, the system still sees the door as open for a few seconds after it closes.
Passive arming, and automatic rearming if no door is opened after disarming, are handy — but the customer must know about them.
Locking the doors when the ignition is switched on or when driving off, and the chirps when arming and disarming — as the customer prefers.
Sensor sensitivity is set on the spot, as in the lesson on sensors, not left at the factory setting. Write everything you set on the installation card.

Remote start, if the system has it, is only for models the manufacturer supports in its compatibility list: for StarLine it’s can.starline.ru, for Pandora the “Table of commands and statuses” on alarmtrade.ru. It is set up per the manufacturer’s instructions: with an automatic transmission the engine starts only with the selector in P; with a manual, software neutral is needed as well. If the model isn’t on the list, we don’t do remote start, as in the lesson on choosing a system.
Testing from a checklist
Arming: arm and disarm from every fob and from the phone — the siren, turn signals, LED and locks respond as set up.
Doors: arm the system and open each door in turn — an alarm, and on a two-way fob or in the app, the door zone. One door that triggers doesn’t prove the others are connected.
Hood and trunk — separately, each one: an alarm and its own indication.
Sensors: after the delay for them to come on, a light slap on a wheel or pillar gives a warning, a harder one an alarm; tilt and interior sensors too, if fitted.
Central locking: all the doors and the trunk lock and unlock — from the fob and from the phone; the factory button and key work as before.
Turn signals: both sides flash — when arming, disarming and during an alarm.
Engine kill: when armed the engine won’t start; after disarming it starts first time. With the engine running, press the fob buttons and open and close a door — the engine must not stall.
GSM: a command from the phone is carried out and the alarm notification arrives. Remote start, if set up, works only under the conditions the manual allows.
Put the interior back together and run through the list once more, briefly.
Test each zone separately and always in the same order — then nothing gets missed.

Key-off current with the alarm

The last measurement is the key-off current: how much the car and the alarm draw from the battery while parked. Measure as in the lesson on parasitic drain: ammeter in the battery negative without breaking the circuit, car locked and armed, hood pin switch held pressed, key well away. Wait for the modules to fall asleep: at first the current is hundreds of milliamps, then it drops. Once asleep, a car with an alarm usually draws tens of milliamps; how much the system itself adds is in its manual, and a GSM module adds more than a basic alarm. Write the result on the installation card: if the customer comes back with a flat battery, you’ll have something to compare against.

Handing the car over is part of the installation, not a formality. A customer who didn’t understand how to disarm will call you at night with the siren wailing — and decide the alarm is no good. Allow 15–20 minutes for the handover: at the car, with the customer’s fob and phone in hand. Run through the checklist once more beforehand, as in the lesson on programming and testing: nothing should fail in front of the customer.
Teach them to use it — at the car
The fob: arming, disarming, car locator, silent arming, the panic button — on the buttons of their own fob. On a two-way fob — what the icons and alarm signals mean.
Have the customer arm the car, open a door, silence the alarm and disarm, all by themselves. What people do with their own hands, they remember.
The app: install and test it on the customer’s phone — commands, alarm notifications, where to check the SIM balance.
Valet mode: during a car wash or repairs the alarm is off, and the fob doesn’t need to be handed over. After the repair the mode is switched off, or the car stays unprotected.

The automatic functions you switched on: passive arming, rearming, locking when driving off. The customer should know about them in advance, not find out with the keys locked inside. If there’s remote start, show how to use it and, with a manual transmission, the software neutral procedure.
Emergency disarming

A fob can break, get lost or end up with a dead battery. For that there is emergency disarming: with the Valet button and a personal PIN code. On many systems each digit is entered as a number of presses on the button with the ignition on — the exact procedure is in the system’s manual. Show the customer where the button is and let them disarm with the code once themselves. Replace the factory code with a personal one: the customer chooses the digits.

Don’t leave a memo with the PIN code or the owner’s card in the car — not in the glove box, not under the floor mat: a thief will find them first. They’re kept at home. Don’t write the code down yourself or put it in your archive.
Warranty and paperwork

Installation report and warranty card: date, system model and serial number, what was installed — modules, sensors, engine kill — warranty periods for the work and the equipment, signatures. The locations of the unit and the kill relay are not written in the customer’s papers.
If the car is under dealer warranty, discuss it with the customer before the installation: the warranty terms for aftermarket equipment are in the service book and at the dealer.
A memo — one page in plain words: arming and disarming, what to do during an alarm, how to disarm without the fob (without the code itself), your phone number.
Give the owner’s card to the customer: it’s used to restore access and to learn new fobs and phones. Lose it, and restoring access gets difficult.
Installation photos — for your own archive

Before reassembling the interior, photograph the unit’s location and its connectors, the power, ground, CAN and pin-switch connection points, the kill relay and the alarm fuses. In the same folder goes the installation card with the settings and the key-off current; label the folder with the plate number and the date. A year later the car comes back with a complaint — from the photos you’ll know where everything is within minutes, without stripping half the interior. Keep the photos to yourself and don’t send them to anyone: they’re a map of where the engine kill is.
Battery drain during long parking

The alarm keeps working while parked, so it always draws current: together with the car, tens of milliamps, as in the lesson on programming and testing. Do the math with the customer: 40 mA is about 1 Ah a day (0.04 × 24), about 20 Ah in three weeks — a third of a 60 Ah battery. In the cold the battery delivers less, and after a long stand the car may not start even though the alarm is fine.

Disconnecting the battery while parked means leaving the car unprotected. It’s the customer’s call, but they need to know.
If the system has a long-parking mode that saves charge, show how to switch it on, per the manual.

Cars with an installed alarm come back with the same complaints over and over. They’re diagnosed like any fault — as in the lesson on the troubleshooting method: ask, confirm, check the simple things, then measure. The photos and installation card from your archive help a lot, as in the lesson on handing the car over: you immediately see where the unit, relay and connection points are. If someone else did the install, start with an inspection: twisted splices, wires without a fuse and connections not done per the manual are obvious right away.

When the alarm is “dead” or one function has gone, I check the fuses first — both the factory ones and the ones in the alarm’s own wiring. Only then do I take off the trim and look at the connections.
Won’t arm

Many systems report which zone is open when you try to arm: with siren chirps or an icon on the fob or in the app — the meanings are in the manual. Most often it’s a pin switch: the system sees a door, the hood or the trunk as open. At the pin-switch input, check with a multimeter or a logic probe whether the signal changes as you open and close, as in the lesson on pin switches. Causes: a corroded or stuck pin switch, a hood switch knocked out of place after a repair, a chafed wire touching the body, water in a connector, a dome light with a fade-out delay. If the system doesn’t respond at all — the fob battery, then the unit’s power and ground.
Example — a ground-side pin switch: the door is closed, yet the input reads 0 V — the unit treats it as open.
Door open — 0 V at the input
Door closed — 12 V: the unit sees “closed”
Door closed, yet 0 V at the input — the unit sees “open”
Start with the alarm memory: the system remembers which zone triggered — on the fob, in the app or by LED flashes. Without it you’re searching blind.
Shock or tilt sensor: sensitivity set too high, the sensor poorly mounted, wind and passing trucks — the settings and the location, as in the lesson on sensors.
Interior sensor: a window or sunroof left ajar, things swinging in the cabin, airflow from the heater.
Doors, hood, trunk: a pin switch with a poor contact or a chafed wire sets off the alarm when the wind rocks the car. The hood switch suffers from dirt and water more than the others.

A poor ground or power feed to the unit: the voltage “wanders” and the unit takes noise for a trigger. The drop on the ground and on the positive is checked with the siren on, as in the lesson on the unit’s power and ground.
Drains the battery
Check the battery itself: charge and condition. An old battery may simply not hold a charge.
Measure the key-off current after the modules fall asleep, as in the lesson on parasitic drain, and compare it with the reading on the installation card.
If the current is higher, find out how much of it the alarm takes: from the voltage drop across its fuse, without pulling it.

The alarm draws a lot: with weak coverage the GSM module keeps searching for the network; the unit can’t sleep because it sees an open door; the kill relay coil is energized for the whole time the car is parked — that’s about 0.1–0.15 A.
The alarm is fine but the car won’t go to sleep — check the CAN module settings: a wrongly configured module can keep the modules awake. After that, hunt for the drain by the usual method.
Central locking doesn’t work

Doesn’t work from the fob but works from the factory button — look in the installation: the fuse and power for the lock outputs, the pulse type, its duration, the contact at the connection point, as in the lesson on central locking.

Doesn’t work from the factory button either: on reversing actuators the wires are cut and routed through the relays’ normally closed contacts. If such a contact corrodes, the locks won’t work from anything — yet the installation is to blame.
Works only sometimes, worse in the cold — the pulse is too short for the actuator or the actuator itself is weak: lengthen the pulse per the manual and check the actuator.
Control over CAN — check the CAN module settings and its connection to the pair, as in the lesson on the CAN bus during installation.
Poor fob range
The fob battery comes first and is the most common cause. Compare with the second fob: if that one reaches farther, the problem is in the first fob.

The antenna: it came unstuck, was moved, its wire got pinched during reassembly, there’s metal nearby or metallized tint — range often drops after tinting, as in the lesson on the siren, antenna and GSM.
Interference: downtown, in a big parking lot, near power lines the range is lower for every system. Check somewhere else — if it’s fine there, it isn’t a fault.
Won’t start because of the engine kill

First make sure the system is disarmed and that the kill isn’t switched on by design — for example, a mode where starting needs a tag or a code — per the manual. Then measure with the ignition on while the pump primes, or while cranking: the voltage before and after the kill relay contact. The same on both sides — the relay isn’t to blame; keep going along the circuit. Voltage before the contact but none after — the relay isn’t passing it: on a normally closed relay the contact is burnt or the coil is getting a signal even though the alarm is disarmed; on a normally open relay the coil isn’t getting its signal. Contacts burn when the relay was chosen without a current margin, as in the lesson on the engine kill. Re-solder any corroded twisted splice in the circuit.

If the starter clicks but doesn’t turn, the engine kill isn’t to blame: it would either have stopped the click or doesn’t affect cranking at all. In that case I give the starter housing a few solid blows with a hammer.
First what the system tells you — the zone or the alarm memory — and the fuses, then measurements along the circuit; archive photos and the card help.
Won’t arm — most often a pin switch: with the door closed, the input must read “closed”.
Drains the battery — key-off current against the handover reading and the drop across the alarm fuse; common culprits are GSM, a unit that won’t sleep, an energized relay coil.
Won’t start — voltage before and after the kill relay contact: present before, missing after — the relay or its control.
The alarm won’t arm and signals that a door is open. Where do you start?
Most often it’s a pin switch or its wire: the system sees the door as open. A measurement at the input shows it right away.
Replace the control unit
Check the pin switches: does the input signal change when you open and close?
Reflash the system
Turn up the shock sensor sensitivity
False alarms at night. What do you look at first?
The alarm memory shows the zone — shock sensor, interior, doors or hood. Without it you’re searching blind.
The alarm memory: which zone triggered
The fob battery
The lock pulse duration
After installation the key-off current went up by about 0.15 A. Which of these looks like the cause?

A typical relay coil draws about 0.1–0.15 A — that’s 17–25 Ah over a week of parking. You need a wiring scheme or setting where the coil is energized only on an attempt to start while armed — per the system’s manual.
The siren is mounted horn facing down
The fob battery is dead
The antenna is stuck next to metal
The kill relay coil is energized for the whole time the car is parked
The alarm is disarmed. 12.4 V before the kill relay contact, 0 V after. Where’s the fault?
Positive reached the relay but went no further. On a normally closed relay — a burnt contact, or a signal on the coil even though the alarm is disarmed.
In the ignition switch
In the kill relay or its control: the contact isn’t passing positive
In the shock sensor

A diesel has no spark plugs: the fuel ignites on its own from the strong compression of hot air. In freezing weather the cold metal soaks up the heat, and without help the engine won’t catch. Three things help: glow plugs, preheating and the right fuel.

These are electric heaters in each cylinder. When you switch on the ignition, a relay or a glow plug control unit powers them, and a yellow coil symbol lights up on the dashboard. While it’s on, the plugs are heating the combustion chambers.
Switch on the ignition and don’t touch the starter until the coil symbol goes out.
Switch off the headlights, the heater and any seat or window heating; with a manual transmission, press the clutch.
Start the engine. If it doesn’t catch, switch off the ignition and heat the glow plugs again.
On many cars the glow plugs keep working after the engine starts, until it warms up: that way it runs more smoothly and smokes less.

Signs of faulty glow plugs: in the cold the starter cranks briskly, but the engine is slow to catch, runs rough for the first few minutes and puts out thick white smoke. On many cars a coil symbol flashing while you drive signals a fault — read the codes. A mechanic will check the glow plugs and the glow plug relay with a multimeter or a clamp meter.
Check the fuses first. If the coil symbol doesn’t light up or the plugs clearly aren’t heating, start by checking the high-current fuse and the glow plug relay.

Many truck diesels — KamAZ, Shacman, Howo — have no glow plugs in the cylinders: in winter an air heater in the intake manifold does the job, either an electric grid heater or a flame-start unit. The procedure is the same: wait for the ready signal on the dashboard.
Engine preheating
A plug-in electric heater running on 220 V mains warms the coolant; it’s usually switched on 1–2 hours before you set off.
A coolant parking heater (Webasto Thermo Top, Eberspächer Hydronic, Binar) warms the engine and the cabin using fuel from the tank, on a timer or from a remote. More on this in the next lesson.
A fuel filter heater keeps the diesel from thickening at the narrowest point.

The extension cord for a 220 V heater must be in good condition, rated for outdoor use, grounded and rated for the heater’s power. Keep the connections dry. Insulation that has cracked in the cold is an electric shock risk.
Winter fuel

Summer diesel turns cloudy in the cold: wax (paraffin) crystals form in it. They clog the fuel filter, and the engine is starved of fuel. Diesel fuel comes in summer (L), off-season (E), winter (Z) and arctic (A) grades. For freezing weather you need winter or arctic fuel — fill up with it at trusted gas stations in advance, before the cold sets in.
Anti-gel (a cold-flow additive) is added before the frost, while the fuel is still clear. It won’t dissolve wax that has already formed.
Don’t dilute diesel with gasoline: it harms modern diesels — the high-pressure fuel pump and the injectors suffer.
Before winter, replace the filter if it’s due, and drain off the water that has settled in it if the filter has a drain valve.
Won’t start in the cold — what to do
The starter cranks sluggishly — it’s the battery: charge it or jump-start it properly, as in the battery lesson.
It cranks briskly but doesn’t catch, and there’s white smoke — suspect the glow plugs: heat them again, then see a mechanic.
After a freezing night it catches and stalls, or doesn’t catch at all — the fuel has probably gelled. Tow the car into a heated garage for a few hours until the wax melts, then replace the filter.
Crank the starter for no more than 10 seconds at a time, with pauses, or you’ll drain the battery.

Don’t heat the filter, fuel lines or tank with an open flame — a blowtorch, a torch or a bonfire: there’s fuel and wiring nearby. Don’t use “quick start” spray unless the owner’s manual allows it: with glow plugs or an intake air heater, the mixture can ignite in the intake and damage the engine.
A diesel starts from compression; in the cold, glow plugs or an intake air heater help it.
Start the engine after the coil symbol goes out; if it doesn’t catch, heat the plugs again.
In winter, use winter or arctic fuel; anti-gel goes in before the frost.
Cranks briskly but won’t catch — glow plugs; catches and stalls after a freezing night — fuel.
No open flames near the fuel system: wax is melted in a heated garage.
In freezing weather, when can you crank the starter on a diesel?
Right after turning the key
After the coil symbol on the dashboard goes out
Only 5 minutes after switching on the ignition
While the coil symbol is on, the glow plugs are heating the combustion chambers. You crank the starter once it goes out; if the engine doesn’t catch, you repeat the preheating.
The starter cranks briskly, the engine won’t catch, and thick white smoke comes out of the exhaust. What does this point to?
A faulty starter
The glow plugs aren’t heating
Brisk cranking means the battery and the starter are fine. White smoke and poor starting in the cold are a typical sign of faulty glow plugs.
When does anti-gel help?
If you add it before the frost, while the fuel is clear
If you add it to fuel that has already gelled
If you pour it into the washer fluid reservoir
The additive stops wax from forming, but it doesn’t dissolve crystals that have already formed. That’s why it’s added in advance.
After a freezing night, wax has formed in the diesel fuel and the engine won’t start. What’s the right thing to do?
Warm the filter with a blowtorch
Dilute the fuel with gasoline
Keep cranking until it starts
Tow the car into a heated garage, then replace the filter
In the warmth the wax will melt on its own. An open flame near the fuel system can end in a fire, and gasoline damages a diesel’s fuel injection system.

A parking heater produces heat without the engine running: it burns fuel from the tank in its own combustion chamber. Air heaters — Planar, Webasto Air Top, Eberspächer Airtronic, Chinese “diesel air heaters” — warm the car interior or the truck cab. Coolant heaters — Webasto Thermo Top, Eberspächer Hydronic, Binar — warm the coolant, and with it the engine and the cabin heater.
How it works

A metering pump feeds small amounts of fuel into the chamber, a glow plug ignites it, a fan blows in air for combustion, and the exhaust goes outside through its own pipe. The control unit monitors the flame, temperature and voltage. If something is wrong, it shuts the heater down and shows a fault code.
How to use it
Switch it on with the control panel, the timer or the remote. Ignition takes a few minutes — that’s normal.

Switch it off only with the button. After that, the heater purges and cools down for a few minutes. While it’s purging, don’t disconnect the battery terminal or turn off the battery master switch on a truck — that’s how parking heaters get overheated and ruined.
Frequent short runs do harm: the chamber doesn’t have time to heat up, and carbon builds up.
In summer, run the heater once a month for about 10 minutes so the pump and the fan don’t seize up.
Turn the heater off at gas stations.

A parking heater’s exhaust is carbon monoxide. Don’t run it in a closed garage, and make sure the exhaust pipe is intact and vents outside. Exhaust smell in the cabin, a headache, drowsiness — switch it off at once, air out the car and see a mechanic. Cheap “diesel air heaters” installed carelessly are especially prone to this.
It’s showing a fault — what to check yourself
Most faults aren’t a breakdown of the heater itself — they come down to power, fuel or air. Check in this order:

Voltage. During ignition the glow plug draws a lot of current, and a weak battery dips below the protection threshold. At rest the battery should read 12,4–12,9 V; on a truck with a 24 V system, twice that — 24,8–25,8 V. Check the terminals too: a corroded contact has the same effect.

Fuel. The heater’s fuel pickup often sits higher than the engine’s, and when the tank is nearly empty the heater can no longer reach the fuel. In winter, keep the tank at least a quarter full. Summer diesel gels first in the heater’s thin fuel line — you need winter fuel, as in the lesson on winter starting.
Air intake and exhaust. Their pipes are outside, under the floor or by the frame: snow, ice and dirt clog them, and a crushed pipe chokes the combustion. Clean and inspect them.
On an air heater — the warm air outlet. A bag or a jacket over the grille, and it goes into an overheating fault.
Check the fuses first. A parking heater usually has its own fuse, often a separate one on the power wire near the battery.

The control panel shows the fault code — as a number on the display or as a number of flashes of the indicator. To find out what it means for your model, see the “Error codes” tab, in the parking heaters section.

After several failed starts in a row, or after overheating, many heaters lock out. The lockout is cleared following the manual or by a mechanic with diagnostic equipment. Don’t keep switching the heater on again and again “just in case it works”: unburned fuel builds up in the chamber.
When to see a mechanic
The fault keeps coming back even though the voltage, fuel and pipes are fine.
Codes for the glow plug, flame sensor, pump, fan or overheating.
Exhaust or fuel smell in the cabin, smoke from under the car, fuel leaks.
The heater is locked out.
Switch it off only with the button; don’t cut the purge short by disconnecting the battery terminal or the master switch.
A common cause of faults is a weak battery: at rest 12,4–12,9 V, on a 24-volt vehicle 24,8–25,8 V.
In winter, keep the tank at least a quarter full, with winter fuel.
The air intake and exhaust are clean and intact; the exhaust vents only outside.
Codes are on the “Error codes” tab; if the fault returns after these checks, or there’s an exhaust smell or a lockout — see a mechanic.
What’s the right way to switch off a parking heater?
Turn off the battery master switch right away so the battery doesn’t drain
With the button on the control panel, then wait for the purge to finish
Disconnect the battery terminal
After you switch it off, the heater purges and cools the chamber. If you cut the power before that, it will overheat and may fail.
In winter the parking heater won’t start, and the tank is almost empty. What’s the most likely cause?
The control unit has burned out
The alternator is faulty
The heater needs to be switched on more often
The heater’s fuel pickup is higher, and it can’t reach the fuel
The heater’s fuel line often draws fuel from higher up than the engine’s pump. With the tank nearly empty, the engine still runs, but the parking heater is already out of fuel.
The heater goes into a voltage fault. What should you check first?
The battery charge and the condition of the terminals
During ignition the heater’s glow plug draws a lot of current. A weak battery or a poor contact at the terminal makes the voltage dip below the protection threshold.
While the parking heater is running, there’s an exhaust smell in the cabin. What should you do?
Open a window a little and ignore it
Turn the heater up to full power
Switch it off, air out the car and go to a mechanic
An exhaust smell means carbon monoxide may be getting into the cabin. It has no color and can poison you without you noticing.

A car alarm with remote start is very handy in winter. But it comes with common complaints: the battery has died, the fob doesn’t respond, the car won’t unlock. You can sort out most of these cases yourself.
Why the battery drains

Remote start on a timer or by temperature, without any driving. Starting in the cold takes a lot of energy from the battery, and 10–20 minutes at idle puts little back. A few days of warm-ups like this, and the battery is dead.
The alarm itself. It draws current all the time, and GSM and GPS modules draw noticeably more. Over a week or two of the car sitting, it adds up.

An installation mistake: the alarm keeps the car’s control units from “going to sleep”, or powers something constantly where it should be powered from the ignition. A parasitic draw test will show it, as in the multimeter lesson.

What helps: drive regularly, at least half an hour at a time, top up the battery with a charger from time to time, and don’t set remote start too often. Many alarms have a low-battery-voltage start feature — it keeps the battery from going completely flat.
The key fob doesn’t work
The fob doesn’t respond or only works up close — first check the fob battery. In the cold, a weak battery gives out faster. Its type is marked inside the fob or in the manual.
The fob works, but the car doesn’t respond and the interior lights don’t come on — the car battery is dead.
The fob has poor range in just one spot — that’s radio interference; move closer.
The fob has “lost” the car after a battery change or a knock — it needs to be paired again following the alarm manual; sometimes only an installer can do this.
How to unlock and start with the key
Take out the mechanical key: on most key fobs it slides out or can be pulled out of the housing.
Unlock the driver’s door. The lock cylinder is sometimes hidden under a cap on the handle — the owner’s manual explains how to remove it.
If the siren goes off, disarm the alarm with the fob or with the emergency override — the Valet button and your PIN code, following the alarm manual.
If the battery is dead, open the hood with the lever inside the car and charge or jump-start the battery, as in the battery lesson.
On a push-button start car with a dead key fob, hold the key against the button or the spot shown in the owner’s manual.
Keep the alarm manual, the spare fob and your PIN code at home, not in the car. When buying a car with an alarm, get all the fobs, the manual and the code from the previous owner.

If the hood has an electric lock, it won’t open when the battery is dead. Ask the installer in advance how to supply power in that case. Don’t cut or bridge the alarm wires to start the car: the immobilizer is designed precisely against that, and repairing the wiring will cost more than calling out the installer.
Check the fuses first. If the alarm shows no signs of life even though the battery is charged, check its own fuse on the power wire.
When you need an installer
The battery started draining after the alarm was installed.
False alarms from wind and passing cars — the shock sensor needs adjusting.
Remote start doesn’t work, or the engine stalls right after it.
After installation, warning lights came on on the dashboard or factory features stopped working.
You need to pair a new key fob.
Remote start without driving drains the battery: starting takes more than warming up gives back.
The fob doesn’t respond — check its battery first; the car doesn’t respond at all — the car battery is dead.
The mechanical key is hidden in the fob; the siren is turned off with the fob or the Valet code, following the manual.
Keep the manual, the code and the spare fob at home.
Parasitic draw after installation, false alarms, remote start failures — see the installer.
For a week the car warmed up on a remote start timer but never went anywhere, and the battery died. Why?
Starting takes more energy than warming up at idle gives back
The key fob broke
That can’t happen — only the alternator is to blame
Starting in the cold drains the battery a lot, and a short run at idle doesn’t have time to make up for it. You need to drive or recharge the battery.
The fob no longer unlocks the car, but when you unlock it with the key, the interior lights come on and everything works. What should you check first?
The key fob battery
The headlight fuse
If the car is alive, the battery is fine. Most often the culprit is a dead fob battery, especially in the cold.
How do you get into the car if the battery is dead?
Break a window
Wait for the battery to recover on its own
Unlock the driver’s door with the mechanical key from the fob
Almost every key fob has a mechanical key. After that, the siren is turned off with the fob or the Valet code, following the manual.
After an alarm was installed, the battery goes flat after a few days of sitting. What should you do?
Fit a bigger battery
Cut the alarm wire
Nothing — that’s how it’s supposed to be
Check the parasitic draw and go back to the installer
A working alarm doesn’t drain the battery in a few days. Increased parasitic draw after installation is a reason to go back to the installer.

You can connect a dashcam, a USB charger, a head unit or auxiliary lights yourself. The main rule: every new load gets its own fuse, and the wire must handle more than that fuse. When running wires from the battery, disconnect the clamp from the negative terminal first.
Work out the current and choose the wire

Current is power divided by voltage. A 5 W dashcam draws less than half an amp. A pair of 55 W lights draws about 110 / 12 ≈ 9 A. The fuse is chosen about a quarter higher than the working current and rounded up to a standard rating: for these lights, 15 A. And the wire gauge is chosen to match the fuse, not the load.

These are conservative figures for stranded copper wire up to 3 m long: 5 A — 0,75 mm², 10 A — 1,5 mm², 15 A — 2,5 mm², 25 A — 4 mm². For a longer wire, or one in a shared harness, go one size thicker. Cheap copper-clad aluminum wire (CCA) of the same thickness carries less current.
Fuse on the positive side, at the source

The fuse goes in the positive wire as close as possible to where you take the power from — the battery or the fuse box. If the wire chafes through against the body, the fuse blows and saves the wiring. If the fuse sits next to the load, the whole wire up to it is unprotected.

Powerful loads — lights, a compressor — are switched through a relay: a switch in the cabin controls the coil (85 and 86), and the high current flows through contacts 30 and 87 over a short, thick wire. How a relay works is covered in the lesson on fuses and relays.
Tapping in with a fuse tap
A dashcam and a USB charger are easy to power from the fuse box with a fuse tap. It plugs into the slot in place of the factory fuse and holds two fuses: the factory one and a new one for your wire.
Buy a fuse tap for your type of fuses: standard, mini or low-profile.
Choose a non-critical circuit that’s powered through the ignition switch, such as the cigarette lighter. That way the dashcam won’t drain the battery while the car is parked.
Pull out the factory fuse, switch on the ignition and use a multimeter to find which side of the slot has 12 V — that’s the power side.
Insert the fuse tap with the blade shared by both fuses on the power side. Put the factory fuse of the same rating into it, plus a new one sized for the device’s current.
Ground goes to the nearest body bolt.

Don’t take power from the airbag (SRS), ABS, engine control unit or fuel pump circuits — neither with a fuse tap nor by splicing into a wire. A fuse tap is only for small things like a dashcam or a charger.
Ground and head unit

The negative goes to bare body metal under a factory bolt, or to the battery negative, with a ring terminal. Plastic, paint and a random self-tapping screw are not a ground: the contact will heat up and the device will glitch.

In a standard ISO connector, the yellow wire is constant positive for memory, the red is switched positive from the ignition, and the black is ground. If both positives are connected to constant power, the head unit will drain the battery. Many cars, especially Japanese ones, have their own connector — buy an adapter for your model instead of cutting the factory wiring.
What not to do
Twisted joints under electrical tape: they corrode, heat up and burn through. Join wires with crimped butt connectors or with solder and heat-shrink tubing.
Connecting to airbag wires, usually in yellow sheathing or with yellow connectors.
Tapping into the CAN bus — a pair of wires twisted together: you’ll get fault codes, and the car may not start.
Taking power or a “control positive” from sensor and control unit signal wires.
Running a wire over sharp edges and through doors without protection; laying the dashcam wire over the curtain airbag in the pillar — route it along the factory harness.
Every new load gets its own fuse in the positive wire, as close to the source as possible.
Current = power / voltage; the wire gauge is chosen to match the fuse.
Powerful loads go through a relay; small ones through a fuse tap in a non-critical circuit switched by the ignition.
Ground goes to clean body metal or the battery negative, with a ring terminal.
No twisted joints, and no tapping into airbags, the CAN bus or sensor wires.
Where does the fuse for a new load go?
In the negative wire, next to the load
In the positive wire, as close to the power source as possible
Nowhere, if the wire is thick
A fuse protects the wire. Placed at the source, it protects the wire along its whole length: if the wire chafes through against the body, the fuse blows before the wiring catches fire.
A pair of 55 W auxiliary lights. Roughly how much current do they draw from a 12 V system?
About 55 A
About 9 A
About 110 A
Current is power divided by voltage: 110 W / 12 V ≈ 9 A. The fuse for them is 15 A, the wire 2,5 mm².
A dashcam was connected with a fuse tap to a circuit that has power all the time. What’s the risk?
The dashcam may drain the battery while the car is parked
None — it’s even better that way
The dashcam will burn out right away
A constant-power circuit stays live even with the engine off. For a dashcam, choose a circuit powered through the ignition switch.
What’s the right way to join wires when connecting something?
Twist them together under electrical tape
Splice into a CAN bus wire
To the airbag connector
With a crimped butt connector, or solder and heat-shrink tubing
A twisted joint corrodes and heats up over time. Crimping, or soldering with heat-shrink tubing, gives a reliable, protected contact.
Drivers can replace most bulbs themselves. But with lighting “upgrades” it’s easy to blind oncoming drivers and break the law.
Bases and bulbs
The bulb type is given in the owner’s manual, on the bulb itself and often on the headlight housing. The most common ones:
H4 — two filaments in one bulb, low and high beam, 60/55 W.
H7, H1, H11 — one filament each, 55 W: low beam, high beam or fog lights.
W5W — a small wedge-base bulb: parking lights, license plate light.
P21W — turn signals, brake lights, reverse lights; P21/5W — dual-filament, brake light and parking light in one bulb; PY21W — amber, for turn signals.
D1S, D2S, D2R, D4S and others with the letter D — factory xenon.
How to replace them
Switch off the lights and the ignition, and let the bulb cool down.
Unplug the connector, remove the protective cap and release the retaining clip.
Hold the new bulb by the base, not the glass: fingerprints make the glass overheat, and the bulb soon burns out.
Seat the bulb exactly in its slots, or the beam will point off to the side, and check that it works.

Replace bulbs in pairs: old ones are dimmer and a different shade. “+50 %” and “+100 %” bulbs of the same 55 W are acceptable if they carry a certification mark — the letter E in a circle — but they don’t last as long. Higher-wattage bulbs, such as 100 W instead of 55, must not be fitted: they melt the headlight and overheat the wiring.
Check the fuses first. If both headlights or both parking lights are out at once, the problem is most likely not the bulbs but a fuse or a relay.
Only touch a xenon bulb and its ballast with the lights off and the connector unplugged: at switch-on there are tens of thousands of volts there, as in the safety lesson.
Xenon and LED in factory headlights

A headlight is designed for its own light source. The lens or housing is marked: the letter H (for example, HC, HCR) means halogen, the letter D (DC, DCR) means xenon. The glowing part of a xenon or LED bulb sits in a different place from a halogen filament, and the reflector spreads the light incorrectly: the road is lit worse, and oncoming drivers are blinded.

In Kazakhstan, xenon or LED bulbs in headlights not designed for them count as unauthorized modification: a fine of 15 MCI (monthly calculation index) under Part 7 of Article 590 of the Code of Administrative Offenses of the Republic of Kazakhstan, and the car can be sent to an impound lot until the factory lighting is restored. The legal route is headlights originally designed for xenon or LED, properly registered according to the rules.

On right-hand-drive cars, the headlights are designed for left-hand traffic: the low-beam cutoff rises to the left, straight into the eyes of oncoming drivers. Such headlights are replaced with ones for right-hand traffic; some can be readjusted — check with a mechanic.
Why LEDs trigger a “bulb out” error

The body control unit monitors the current of each bulb. A 21 W halogen bulb draws about 1,75 A; an LED replacement draws many times less. The unit decides the bulb has burned out: a warning appears on the dashboard, the turn signals flash faster, and the LED may flicker from the unit’s test pulses.

So-called “error cancellers” are sold — load resistors and bulbs marked CANbus. A resistor turns the excess current into heat and gets very hot: never mount it on plastic or wires. Factory bulbs or a mechanic are a safer bet — sometimes the unit can be reconfigured with a scan tool.
Headlight aim

Use the headlight leveling knob on the dashboard to lower the beams when the car is loaded; which position suits which load is in the owner’s manual. You can roughly check the aim against a wall: level ground, normal tire pressure, the leveler at “0”, the car 5 m from the wall. Mark the height of the headlight centers on the wall: the low-beam cutoff should be below it. If the headlight is marked with a 1 % tilt, at 5 m that’s 5 cm. Headlights are aimed precisely at a service station with an aiming device.
The bulb type is in the owner’s manual and on the bulb; hold halogen bulbs by the base and replace them in pairs.
Both headlights out at once — check the fuse and relay first.
Xenon and LED only in headlights designed for them; otherwise they blind oncoming drivers and can get you a 15 MCI fine.
LEDs in a factory circuit trigger an error because of their low current; “error canceller” resistors get very hot.
The low-beam cutoff is below the headlight centers: with a 1 % tilt, 5 cm lower at 5 m.
Why shouldn’t you touch the glass of a halogen bulb with your fingers?
Fingerprints make the glass overheat, and the bulb soon burns out
You could get an electric shock
The bulb will start glowing blue
The greasy mark creates a hot spot on the glass. The glass overheats, and the bulb burns out much sooner than it should.
Can you put LED bulbs in a headlight marked HCR?
Yes, if the base fits
No: the headlight is designed for halogen, LEDs blind oncoming drivers, and you can be fined for it
Yes, if you add a resistor
The letter H means the headlight is designed for halogen bulbs. With a different light source it spreads the light incorrectly, and in Kazakhstan this counts as unauthorized modification.
After LEDs were fitted in the turn signals, they flash faster and there’s a warning on the dashboard. Why?
The alternator has burned out
The wrong LED color
Positive and negative are mixed up
The LED draws little current, and the control unit thinks the bulb has burned out
The control unit or the turn signal relay monitors the current. An LED draws many times less than a halogen bulb, and the electronics take this as a burned-out bulb.
Both low-beam headlights are out at once. What should you check first?
Buy new headlights
The headlight leveler position
The low-beam fuse and relay
Two bulbs rarely burn out at the same time. The common cause for both is a fuse, a relay or the power supply.

Most roadside breakdowns start with something small you could have spotted at home: a corroded terminal, a cracked belt, a burned-out bulb. Twenty minutes of checks before a trip or before winter will save you a long wait on the side of the road.
Battery and terminals
Voltage after sitting overnight: 12,6–12,9 V. At about 12,4 V or below, charge it before the trip.
With the engine running: 13,5–14,5 V, including with the headlights and the heater on. If it’s lower, check the alternator before you set off.
The terminals shouldn’t turn by hand. If there’s a white or green coating, remove the clamp, clean it with a brush, wipe it with a baking soda solution and tighten it.
The battery is firmly secured and doesn’t move around.
A battery usually lasts 3–5 years. If yours is more than 4 years old or has already let you down, have a mechanic check it with a load tester before winter.
Alternator belt

Cracks across the ribs, peeling layers, a shiny “glazed” surface — it’s time to replace the belt. A squeal when starting in the cold or when a load is switched on means the belt is slipping: low tension, a worn tensioner or a worn belt. A snapped belt means a draining battery, and on many cars the water pump stops too and the engine overheats. If the battery light comes on while you’re driving, the alternator isn’t charging, as in the lesson on dashboard warning lights.
Inspect the belt only with the engine off and the ignition off: the radiator fan can switch on by itself. Keep your hands away from the belt and pulleys of a running engine.
Lights and fuses

Walk around the car: low and high beams, parking lights, turn signals, hazard lights, brake lights, reverse lights, license plate light, fog lights. Someone can help you check the brake lights, or you can look at their reflection in a shop window in the evening. Take spare bulbs of your types, as in the lighting lesson.

Put spare fuses of your type — standard, mini or low-profile — and a pair of tweezers in the glove box. Take photos of the diagrams on the fuse box lids with your phone: in the dark and the cold, it’s quicker that way.
Check the fuses first. Many roadside “breakdowns” are fixed in five minutes with a spare fuse of the same rating.
Before winter — extra checks
Fully charge the battery with a charger, even if the car starts.
On a diesel — glow plugs, winter fuel and the filter, as in the lesson on winter starting.
Run the parking heater before the cold sets in, so any faults show up now and not at −30 °C.
Check the heater fan at all speeds, the window and mirror heating, the wipers and the washer, and fill up with winter washer fluid.
Replace the key fob battery if its range has got worse.
What to take with you

Jumper cables 3–4 m long with copper conductors: from 16 mm² for a car, from 25 mm² for a diesel or an SUV. Cheap cables have thick insulation but a thin conductor — look at the copper, not the sheathing.
A jump starter (booster) — charged. In winter, keep it inside the car: lithium jump starters get noticeably weaker in the cold.
A multimeter or a test light, spare fuses and bulbs.
A headlamp, gloves, electrical tape, cable ties and a wrench for the battery terminals — on many cars it’s a 10 mm.
A phone charger for the cigarette lighter socket, a tow rope, warm clothes. A fire extinguisher, a first-aid kit and a warning triangle are mandatory.
Battery: 12,6–12,9 V at rest and 13,5–14,5 V while driving; the terminals are clean and don’t turn.
A belt with no cracks, glazing or squeal; inspect it only with the engine off.
All the lights work; spare bulbs and fuses are in the car.
Before winter — fully charge the battery and check the parking heater, glow plugs and heating functions.
For the road — thick copper jumper cables or a jump starter, a flashlight, a multimeter, tools.
Before winter, the battery reads 12,3 V after sitting overnight. What should you do?
Nothing, that’s normal
Charge it with a charger and check again
Replace the alternator right away
Full charge is 12,6–12,9 V. At 12,3 V the battery is noticeably discharged, and in freezing weather it will need all the reserve it has.
The alternator belt squeals when starting in the cold. What does that mean?
That’s normal in winter
The belt is slipping: tension, the tensioner or a worn belt
A squeal means slipping. If the cause isn’t fixed, the alternator will undercharge the battery, and the belt may snap.
Which jumper cables should you take for a diesel SUV?
Copper, with a cross-section of 25 mm² or more
Any thin ones, as long as they’re long
With thick sheathing; the cross-section doesn’t matter
A diesel needs a lot of current to start. A thin conductor under thick insulation heats up and can’t carry it.
How do you inspect the alternator belt safely?
At idle, so you can see it slipping
With the ignition on
Holding the belt with your hand while the engine runs
With the engine off and the ignition off
On a running engine, the belt can pull your hand in, and with the ignition on, the radiator fan can switch on by itself.

The starter is the most powerful load in the car: it draws hundreds of amps while cranking. That’s why a few extra hundredths of an ohm in its circuit immediately turn into slow cranking. The diagnostician’s job is to work out whether the starter itself, its power supply or its control circuit is to blame.
How it’s built
Electric motor: an armature with a commutator, brushes, and a stator with field windings or permanent magnets.

The solenoid on the housing. It has two windings — pull-in and hold-in. Through a shift fork, the solenoid pushes the pinion into mesh with the flywheel ring gear and, at the end of its travel, closes the main contacts (the “contact discs”) between terminal 30 and the motor.
The Bendix drive is a pinion with an overrunning clutch. Once the engine starts, the clutch slips and keeps the engine from overspinning the armature.
Gear-reduction starter: a planetary gearset sits between the motor and the pinion; the motor is small and fast, often with permanent magnets. This type of starter is lighter and draws less current.

A heavy power cable runs from the battery to terminal 30, usually with no fuse. Terminal 50 gets positive from the ignition switch, and on most modern cars it comes through a starter relay controlled by the ignition switch, the body control module or the ECU. Interlocks are wired into the circuit: the automatic transmission range switch (starting only in P or N), on many cars a clutch pedal switch, and on cars with a start button, the brake pedal.
The battery is charged: 12,4–12,9 V at rest. With a discharged battery, there’s no point measuring any further.

To keep the engine from starting during the measurements, disable the fuel supply as the manual describes — for example, pull the fuel pump fuse or relay. Set the parking brake and put the automatic in P.
Terminal 50: with the key in START, the voltage is almost the same as at the battery while cranking. No positive — look in the control circuit: fuse, relay, interlocks, ignition switch.

Drop on the positive side while cranking (as in the multimeter lesson): from the battery’s positive post to terminal 30 — up to 0,5 V. On the ground side: from the starter housing to the battery’s negative post — up to 0,2–0,3 V.
Battery voltage while cranking — no lower than about 9,6–10 V.

Cranking current — measure it with a clamp meter on the power cable. For gasoline passenger cars it’s usually around 100–200 A, more for diesels; the spec is in the manual. Shacman, Howo and KAMAZ trucks have a 24 V system with their own specs.

High current and slow cranking — mechanical resistance: bushings, a short in the armature, a tight engine. Low current and slow cranking — resistance in the circuit: terminals, wires, the “contact discs”, brushes.
A click with no rotation: burnt solenoid contacts, worn or stuck brushes, a “dead spot” on the commutator.
The starter whirs but doesn’t turn the engine: the overrunning clutch is slipping or the pinion isn’t coming out. The fix is to replace the Bendix drive and inspect the ring gear teeth.
Grinding or seizing in a gear-reduction starter — the gearset has failed or a magnet has come unglued.
The starter keeps cranking after the key is released — the solenoid contacts are stuck closed. Turn off the ignition; if it keeps spinning, disconnect the battery negative.
If it cranks after a few taps, the starter is worn and due for repair: brushes, solenoid contacts, bushings.

Disconnect the battery negative before removing the starter: terminal 30 is always live, and a wrench touching the housing will cause a short of hundreds of amps — burns and fire. Don’t run the starter by bridging terminals 30 and 50 with a screwdriver: this bypasses the interlocks, and a car in gear will drive off. Crank for no more than 10 seconds at a time, with 30–60 second pauses.
The solenoid pushes the Bendix drive into mesh and closes the main contacts from 30 to the motor.
No positive at 50 when starting — look in the control circuit: relay, automatic transmission and clutch interlocks, ignition switch.
While cranking: up to 0,5 V on the positive side, up to 0,2–0,3 V on the ground side, battery no lower than about 9,6–10 V.
High current and slow — mechanical; low current and slow — resistance in the circuit.
With the key turned to START, there’s no voltage at starter terminal 50. Where should you look?
In the starter brushes
In the Bendix overrunning clutch
In the control circuit: fuse, starter relay, transmission or clutch interlock, ignition switch
Terminal 50 is the control input. If positive doesn’t reach it, the starter itself isn’t to blame: the cause is in the circuit leading to it.
The starter cranks slowly, the cranking current is noticeably above spec, and the drops on the positive and ground sides are normal. What is most likely?
Mechanical resistance: bushings, a short in the armature or an engine that’s hard to turn
A corroded battery terminal
An open in the terminal 50 wire
A bad contact would reduce the current. High current with slow rotation means the motor is struggling to turn.
The starter whirs loudly, but the engine doesn’t turn over. What is most likely faulty?
The Bendix overrunning clutch or the pinion engagement mechanism
Control circuit fuse
The starter motor spins, so power and control are fine. The rotation isn’t reaching the flywheel.
How do you measure the voltage drop on the starter ground?
Red lead on terminal 30, black on terminal 50
Both leads on the starter housing with the ignition off
Red on the battery negative, black on the body, with no load
Red on the starter housing, black on the battery’s negative post — while cranking
The drop is measured under load, between the load’s housing and the battery negative. With no current flowing, a bad contact doesn’t show up.

Misfires are one of the most common complaints: the engine runs rough, jerks under load, and the “Check Engine” light comes on or flashes. The cause can be ignition, fuel or mechanical. The goal isn’t to replace everything in sight, but to find the cause in a few checks.
What’s on the engine
Individual coils — one for each spark plug. The most common setup on modern Toyota, Hyundai, Kia and Chinese cars.
A module or twin coils serving two cylinders, with high-voltage leads — “wasted spark”: the spark fires in two cylinders at once, and one of them is on its exhaust stroke.

A coil with two terminals has no igniter: the ECU itself switches the ground of the primary winding. One with three or four terminals usually has a built-in igniter: positive, ground, the control signal from the ECU, and sometimes a spark confirmation signal (IGF on Toyota). Pin functions — only from the wiring diagram.

Type, gap and heat range — strictly per the manual or catalog. Heat range scales differ between manufacturers, some even run in opposite directions, so you can’t compare plugs from different brands “by the number”.
Check the gap with a round wire gauge. Plugs with a fine iridium or platinum electrode are usually installed with the factory gap; don’t bend the center electrode. Tightening torque — per the manual.

Read the insulator: light brown — normal; dry black soot — rich mixture or weak spark; wet with fuel — the cylinder is misfiring; oil — worn rings or valve stem seals; white and blistered — overheating; a crack or a flashover “track” — replace the plug.
How to find misfires

Read the codes: P0300 — misfires in random or multiple cylinders, P0301–P0306 — a misfire in the cylinder whose number is the last digit. A flashing “Check Engine” light means misfires bad enough to overheat the catalytic converter: don’t keep driving like that for long.
Look at the freeze frame — the rpm, load and temperature at which the misfires appeared — and the per-cylinder misfire counters, if your scan tool shows them.
Inspect the spark plug wells: oil from under the valve cover gasket or water after a car wash destroys the coil boots.
Swap the coils of the suspect cylinder and a neighboring one, as in the lesson on actuators. If the misfire follows the coil, the coil is to blame. If it stays, swap the spark plugs the same way.
If the misfire stays put, check the injector and its wiring, the compression and the valves.
Checking the coil circuits
Positive at the coil connector — with the ignition on or while cranking. Check the ground by voltage drop under load, relative to the battery negative.
The signal from the ECU to a coil with an igniter — check it with an LED test light or an oscilloscope while cranking: you should see even pulses.

In the primary circuit of a coil without an igniter, spikes of hundreds of volts occur when the circuit opens. Don’t connect an LED test light or a test lamp there — only an oscilloscope with an attenuator.
No signal at all the coils at once — check the crankshaft position sensor and the ECU’s power supply and grounds.

The secondary circuit carries tens of thousands of volts. Remove coils only with the ignition off, don’t hold the leads by hand with the engine running, and don’t check for spark “to ground” without a spark tester: the spark will find a path through the insulation and damage the coil and the ECU, and the shock is dangerous — especially for people with a pacemaker.
P0300 — misfires in multiple cylinders, P0301–P0306 — the cylinder number is the last digit.
Flashing “Check Engine” — severe misfires, the catalytic converter is at risk.
Swapping coils and spark plugs shows whether the fault follows the part.
Spark plug gap and heat range — only per the manual or catalog.
The secondary circuit carries tens of kilovolts: remove coils with the ignition off and check for spark with a spark tester.
What does code P0304 mean?
Misfires in cylinder 4
The cylinder 4 coil is faulty
The code points to misfires in a cylinder, not to a part. The coil, spark plug, injector or compression could be to blame.
The coils of cylinders 2 and 3 were swapped, and code P0302 changed to P0303. What’s faulty?
The cylinder 2 spark plug
The cylinder 3 injector
The coil that used to be on cylinder 2
The misfire moved with the coil, so the coil is the problem.
Why can’t you choose the heat range by comparing the numbers on plugs from different manufacturers?
That number means the gap
Manufacturers use different scales, sometimes opposite ones — choose only by the catalog or manual
Heat range doesn’t affect anything
For one brand a higher number means a colder plug, for another a hotter one. A mistake leads to carbon fouling or overheating.
How do you safely check for spark?
Hold the lead near the body with your hand
Remove the coil with the engine running
Measure the resistance of a coil with a built-in igniter
Connect a spark tester to the coil and crank the engine
A spark tester gives the spark a safe path. An ohmmeter won’t tell you anything about a coil with an igniter.
Many “faulty” ECUs are actually fine: they’re short of power or ground. Before looking for the cause in the sensors and injectors, make sure the module is properly powered.
How the engine module is powered
+30 — constant positive from the battery through a fuse. It keeps the memory alive: adaptations and trouble codes.
+15 — positive after the ignition switch. For the module, this is the “wake up” command.

The main relay. On many cars, once the ECU gets +15, it switches on the relay coil itself, and power from contact 87 goes to the module and to the injectors, coils, oxygen sensor heaters and sensors. After the ignition is turned off, the module keeps the relay on for a few seconds or longer — to save data and keep the fan running for a while.

The fuel pump relay is also switched by the ECU. On many cars, when the ignition is switched on, the pump runs for 2–3 seconds and shuts off if the module doesn’t see the crankshaft turning. Some cars have a fuel pump control module instead of a relay.
Engine and body grounds

An ECU usually has several grounds: power grounds for the injectors and coils, and signal grounds. Many sensors get their ground and 5 V reference from the module itself: don’t short these wires to the body. The engine, body and battery negative are connected by ground straps. A corroded or broken strap causes intermittent codes from many sensors at once.
Measure under load: while cranking, or with the engine running and the headlights and fan on.
Module ground: red lead on the ground pin of the ECU connector from the wire side, black on the battery’s negative post. Normal is hundredths of a volt; more than 0,1 V — look for a bad contact.
Engine ground: red lead on the cylinder block, black on the battery negative, while cranking. Guideline — up to 0,2–0,3 V.
+B supply with the relay on — almost the same as at the battery. A noticeable difference — look for losses section by section: fuse, the 30–87 contact, connector.
Positive comes from the main relay; the ECU switches the ground. Resistance — per the manual; injectors on the same engine should read almost the same.
The pulse from the ECU — check it with an injector noid light while cranking or with an oscilloscope, as in the oscilloscope lesson. Pulse width — per the manual and live data.
No pulses at any injector — check the main relay, the ECU’s power and grounds, the crankshaft sensor signal and immobilizer codes. None at one injector — check its wire and the module pin.
The sequence: fuse and relay, then positive and ground at the pump connector under load, current with a clamp meter and fuel pressure with a gauge — specs per the manual.

The fuel in the lines is under pressure. Relieve the pressure as the manual describes, don’t disconnect the line while the pump is running, keep a fire extinguisher nearby and don’t allow sparks near fuel.
How not to damage the ECU
Disconnect and connect the module connector only with the ignition off and the battery negative disconnected.
Discharge static by touching body ground; on the bench, wear an antistatic wrist strap.
Don’t pierce the insulation with needles unless you have to: come in with a thin probe from the wire side through the seal, or use a breakout adapter. If you did pierce it, seal it.
Don’t connect a test lamp to ECU pins and sensor circuits, and don’t apply 12 V to 5 V circuits.
The ECU is powered from +30, +15 and the main relay; on many cars the module switches the relay itself.
ECU ground under load — hundredths of a volt; more than 0,1 V — a bad contact.
No pulses at any of the injectors — first check power, grounds and the crankshaft sensor.
